crude.up_what: Importer currencies tend to weaken against the dollar, and exporter currencies tend to firm.
crude.up_view: List the foreign-currency payments you owe on imports that are not yet hedged, and check that your current hedges match the amounts and dates of the next payment cycle.
crude.down_what: Importer currencies tend to firm against the dollar, and exporter currencies tend to ease.
crude.down_view: Do not close out hedges because of one price move; first test whether your hedged share of each exposure still fits the updated forecast.

exporter.up_what: Your crude sales are priced in dollars, so higher prices raise your dollar revenue. If your home currency firms against the dollar, part of that gain is lost when you convert.
exporter.up_view: Compare expected dollar revenue with your local-currency costs, and check that hedges on future crude sales still match the volumes and dates you expect to sell.
exporter.down_what: Your dollar revenue falls with the price, and exporter currencies tend to ease against the dollar, which softens the loss when you convert.
exporter.down_view: Recalculate expected dollar revenue at the lower price, and check what share of future sales is hedged, so the budget does not rely on the earlier price.

crude.up_what: Higher crude lifts headline inflation, which can keep central banks tighter for longer.
crude.up_view: Before the next central-bank decisions, calculate floating-rate interest cost under a scenario where interest rates stay high for longer than expected.
crude.down_what: Lower crude eases headline inflation and can give central banks room to pause.
crude.down_view: Confirm that your plans to borrow at a fixed rate are unchanged; one price move does not show where central banks will set interest rates.

exporter.up_what: Higher crude brings in more cash, so borrowing needs may fall. Higher inflation can keep central banks tighter for longer, so rates on any debt you hold stay high.
exporter.up_view: Check whether the extra cash lets you repay floating-rate debt early or borrow less, and compare the interest saved with the yield from keeping the cash on deposit.
exporter.down_what: Lower crude brings in less cash, so borrowing needs may rise. Easing inflation can give central banks room to cut rates, but the cuts may come slowly.
exporter.down_view: Recalculate cash flow at the lower price, and test whether debt repayments are still covered if interest rates fall only slowly.

crude.up_what: Fuel and input costs rise, so cash tied up in inventory and receivables grows.
crude.up_view: Confirm that your committed credit lines are large enough for the bigger swing in working capital, and calculate what drawing on them would cost at current short-term interest rates.
crude.down_what: Working-capital needs ease, and released cash sits in short-term deposits.
crude.down_view: Update the cash forecast first, then invest any cash that is freed up within the investment policy's limits on maturity and counterparty.

exporter.up_what: Amounts owed to you by buyers grow with the price, so more cash is tied up until buyers pay.
exporter.up_view: Check the credit limit and payment terms you give each buyer, and follow up late invoices quickly, because each late invoice is now larger.
exporter.down_what: Receivables and stock are worth less at the lower price, so less cash is released and total cash inflow falls.
exporter.down_view: Update the cash forecast at the lower price, then check that committed credit lines and cash reserves still cover fixed costs and debt payments.

crude.up_what: Commodity hedges settle daily, so on positions that lose when prices rise, a sharp move can call for cash within a day.
crude.up_view: Check that the cash you hold to meet variation margin calls (daily top-up payments on hedging contracts) is enough, and who is authorised to approve a same-day transfer.
crude.down_what: On positions that lose when prices fall, the margin call comes on the way down instead.
crude.down_view: Identify which hedges lose value if the price falls, and confirm that your cash buffer for margin calls and your same-day approval process can still cope.

exporter.up_what: If you hedged future crude sales, those hedges lose value when prices rise and daily margin payments may be needed, while your physical sales gain.
exporter.up_view: Check that you hold enough cash to meet daily margin calls on hedges that lose value when prices rise, and who is authorised to approve a same-day transfer.
exporter.down_what: Hedges on future sales gain value when prices fall, which offsets part of the lower revenue, and margin cash may be returned to you.
exporter.down_view: Count a hedge gain in the forecast only once it is settled in cash, and check that each hedge still matches the volumes you expect to sell.

crude.up_what: Energy-heavy customers and suppliers come under pressure, while producers' credit tends to improve.
crude.up_view: Rank your counterparties again by how much their business depends on energy prices, and review credit limits for those you give long payment terms.
crude.down_what: Producers come under pressure, while energy-heavy users get relief.
crude.down_view: Rank your counterparties again, starting with energy producers, and review credit limits for those you give long payment terms.

exporter.up_what: Buyers whose costs depend on crude, such as airlines and refiners, may come under pressure and pay late, while your own credit standing tends to improve.
exporter.up_view: Rank your buyers again by how much crude costs weigh on their business, and review credit limits and payment terms for those under most pressure.
exporter.down_what: Your own credit standing weakens as revenue falls, and lenders may look harder at your accounts, while buyers that use crude gain relief.
exporter.down_view: Test the financial covenants (the financial tests in your loan agreements) against lower-price forecasts, and talk to lenders early if any covenant could be breached.

points.head: Qatar money markets
points.text: QCB raised its deposit, repo and lending rates by 25 bp each from 17 September, to 4.10%, 4.35% and 4.60%. The deposit rate now sits above both SOFR (3.88%) and the top of the Fed range (4.00%), with the riyal pegged at QAR 3.64 per USD.
points.view: Before placing surplus cash, compare riyal deposit yields with dollar deposit yields for the same maturity, and keep counterparty limits unchanged while yields rise.

importer.label: Crude importer
importer.def: Crude importer: you buy crude oil or fuel, or your costs rise with it, such as airlines, refiners and fuel buyers.

exporter.label: Crude exporter
exporter.def: Crude exporter: you sell crude oil, or your revenue rises with it, such as producers and traders of crude.
